findings.draft_passage: For my mind was made up to sail in no other than a Nantucket craft.
findings.source_has: it may as well be related that I, for one, had no idea of so doing [stopping at New Bedford to embark]. For my mind was made up to sail in no other than a Nantucket craft
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely misled: the causal 'For' appears to explain why Ishmael accepted the delay in New Bedford, but it actually explains a conclusion (that he never planned to embark from New Bedford) that was cut from the draft, leaving the logical pivot without its target.

findings.draft_passage: that he should lie stranded before the door of Dives is more wonderful than that an iceberg should be moored to one of the Moluccas.
findings.source_has: says old Dives, in his red silken wrapper—(he had a redder one afterwards) pooh, pooh! … Now, that Lazarus should lie stranded there on the curbstone before the door of Dives
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: 'Dives' appears without introduction in the draft — the source's earlier sentence naming and characterising Dives was cut from the Euroclydon passage, so a reader has no basis for knowing who or what 'Dives' refers to.

findings.draft_passage: strangely heightened by Elijah's diabolical incoherences uninvitedly recurring to me.
findings.source_has: strangely heightened at times by the ragged Elijah's diabolical incoherences uninvitedly recurring to me … that outlandish prophet of the wharves
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader with no source access has no way to know who Elijah is — the draft provides no appositive, descriptor, or prior introduction in any surviving draft chapter, so the name is genuinely unplaceable, not merely less evocative.

findings.draft_passage: but gave the captain to understand distinctly, that his death would be the signal for a murderous mutiny on the part of all hands.
findings.source_has: but gave the captain to understand distinctly, that his (Steelkilt's) death would be the signal for a murderous mutiny on the part of all hands.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: 'his' follows 'the captain' as the nearest explicit noun, making the captain's death the more natural grammatical reading, but the intended referent is Steelkilt — the parenthetical '(Steelkilt's)' that the draft cut was the only disambiguation.

findings.draft_passage: the line blisteringly passed through both of Stubb's hands, from which the hand-cloths had accidentally dropped — like holding an enemy's sharp two-edged sword by the blade.
findings.source_has: It blisteringly passed through and through both of Stubb's hands, from which the hand-cloths, or squares of quilted canvas sometimes worn at these times, had accidentally dropped.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: 'hand-cloths' is a technical term whose meaning and protective function are never established in the draft, so the reader cannot understand why their absence is consequential — the entire point of the detail (bare hands on a burning line) is lost without the gloss.

findings.source_has: Cook replies "Who dat? Den preach to him yourself," turning to leave; Stubb then says "No, cook; go on, go on." — the cook's exit-line that triggers Stubb's rejoinder was cut, leaving Stubb's line without a triggering speech.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader genuinely cannot tell what Stubb is responding to — 'No' implies a refusal of something the cook said or did, but no such speech or action precedes it in the draft; the reader is actually confused, not merely reading a less-ornamented version.

findings.draft_passage: But I never look at Fedallah at all; if ever I get a chance of a dark night, and he standing hard by the bulwarks, and no one by—look down there, Flask—Aye, will I!
findings.source_has: In the source this 'I never look at him at all' opens Stubb's speech about Fedallah, contrasting with the preceding 'Sink him!'—before the flag-ship story. In the draft it is appended after the flag-ship/cholera anecdote, making 'But I never look at Fedallah at all' a contrast with nothing in the immediately preceding text.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: Stubb has just finished the flag-ship story and the cholera punchline, then abruptly says 'But I never look at Fedallah at all'—the 'But' implies a contradiction of a preceding claim that Stubb watches or engages with Fedallah, yet no such claim appears in the draft; it is one side of a two-sided contrast whose other side was cut.

findings.draft_passage: "But Stubb, you boasted of giving Fedallah a sea-toss; if he's going to live for ever, what good will pitching him overboard do?"
findings.source_has: In the source this line is preceded by Stubb's extended mainmast/hoops speech establishing that Fedallah is immortally old ('well, that wouldn't begin to be Fedallah's age'), which gives Flask's 'if he's going to live for ever' its logical premise. That speech was cut from the draft.
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader of the draft has been given no basis for Flask's conditional 'if he's going to live for ever' — Stubb never argued this in the draft — so the sentence reads as Flask rebutting a claim that was never made, genuinely confusing the logical structure of the exchange.

findings.draft_passage: "Nail-stubbs of the steel shoes of racing horses."
findings.source_has: "Look ye, blacksmith, these are the gathered nail-stubbs of the steel shoes of racing horses."
findings.gate_test_answer: A reader is genuinely confused: the utterance has no main verb and no subject, leaving it a bare noun phrase that does not parse as a sentence or a recognisable exclamatory fragment—the compression stripped the predicate ('these are') that made it grammatical.
